publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Low Bit Rate Image Coding

articleTitle: Image coding using an analysis-synthesis technique
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Low Bit Rate Image Coding
abstract: Model-based coding is becoming an important technique for image data compression. One approach is specific to images containing a particular domain of objects such as a human head-and-shoulders. A computer model of a head-and-shoulders is generated by analysing a sequence of images and locating a set of important feature points. Image texture is mapped onto the model which is used to generate a sequence of moving synthetic images. Motion in the synthetic image is made to approximate the motion in the original sequence by tracking feature points. The paper describes simulation work on this type of model-based coding. It also discusses the analysis aspects of a model-based coding system for videophone images.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Low Bit Rate Image Coding
abstract: Region and texture coding is a second generation technique that uses features identified in the original picture to decompose it into two components which are then coded separately. The purpose of taking this approach is that by finding and encoding the perceptually important features of the image they will be preserved. By separating the signal into two components of very different character it should be possible to design efficient coders for each of them. The paper is a comparative study of three techniques that can be employed to code the region signal. The authors detail how the region signal is generated and three algorithms which can be used to code it. A comparative experiment is performed and the results presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Low Bit Rate Image Coding
abstract: Describes a patented technique, which is capable of determining the location of a face within a video phone image by means of vector coding, and has been successfully demonstrated on video sequences such as Miss America. While the technique is described within the scenario of locating a face the technique could well be applied hierarchically to parts of the face such as the eyes, nose and mouth, or indeed to any other predefined object.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Low Bit Rate Image Coding
abstract: Proposes an alternative coding scheme which is based on a new criterion as well as a new image model. The main goal for image coding should be to preserve the essential structure of lines or shapes. From this point of view the code-book design is focused on representation of edges, not only because of their perceptual importance but also because edges are the most basic transition elements which can be used to construct various waveforms. Taking into account the statistics of edges in images, the authors propose an 8-class, 16-vector code-book (two vectors per class) which results from a training sequence using the LBG algorithm (the training pictures used are 'Boat' and 'Flowers').<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Spatial domain coding techniques for image sequences
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Low Bit Rate Image Coding
abstract: Two spatial domain techniques for coding videotelephone images are described. These coders are considered as part of a class of coders which try to preserve the visually important features of the image by employing image analysis techniques and characteristics such as those of the human visual system. Since high sensitivity to image edges is one of the main features of the human eye an important property of two component and segmented image coders can be considered to be their different treatment of the image components, paying special attention to the edge component. It is possible, therefore, to restrict the distortion to the edge component and preserve the sharpness of the image. This is not the case with conventional coders, however, as the whole image is treated in a uniform way. To demonstrate the efficiency of the above coding algorithms comparisons have been made with the results of the conventional DCT coding technique commonly used.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Low Bit Rate Image Coding
abstract: Illustrates the value of contours of constant intensity in the compression of digital images. Contours have been used for many years in cartography, where a sparse set of smooth connected curves convey a very accurate impression of the landscape. The compression ratios of existing coding techniques appear to have reached a saturation level of about 10:1. It has been suggested, Kunt (1985), that in order to make further significant advances in image coding it will be necessary to adopt radical new approaches in which scene content is explicitly coded. The author suggests the use of contours of constant intensity as the primitives to be extracted both for image coding purposes and image analysis. Images are coded by retaining a set of contours describing the scene content. The images are then reconstructed by interpolating between the contours.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A progressive encoding technique for binary images
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Low Bit Rate Image Coding
abstract: A major problem with modern document processing systems which incorporate high resolution workstations for displaying images is that the resolution of the stored image is often far greater than the resolution at which it is to be displayed. In contemporary systems an image must be fully decompressed and then have its resolution transformed in order to be displayed as required. The authors present a novel technique for performing compression of binary images which uses progressive encoding. The compression is noiseless, and the progressive encoding allows a low resolution rendition of an image to be reconstructed at a minimal complexity.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Image coding for high resolution remote sensing imaging instruments
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Low Bit Rate Image Coding
abstract: Remote sensing and scientific instruments are generating increasing volumes of data which has to be sent back to Earth for processing, interpretation and dissemination to end users. Telemetry links with limited bandwidth form a communications bottleneck for transferring the large amounts of data collected to ground. Data compression and other data rate reduction techniques are becoming vital to the success of future missions. The paper assesses the data compression requirements of present and future high resolution space-based imaging instruments. A brief review is made of several promising image coding techniques for use on remote sensing images. The importance of the effect of image data compression on subsequent processing algorithms is stressed and the constraints on technology for use in on-board image coding systems are explained.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: State of the art in low bit rate image coding
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Low Bit Rate Image Coding
abstract: There has been tremendous interest in low bit rate image coding over the past few years and a multitude of reports both in the general and technical literature about the technology and the impact it will have on business and the individual consumer. The paper provides an overview of directions for the future, particularly with regard to the development of standards. It is clear that there has been considerable interest in the use of photographic images, in a diverse range of applications, as digital technology advances and becomes more widely available. The proliferation of different approaches to image coding has created a number of challenges for the industry and the technology will look very different in the 21st century than it does today. The technology will have a significant impact on our lives in a similar way to the telephone and facsimile machines, and the way they have affected our lives today. For one thing, the sharp division between video processing, computers and document image processing will become blurred as the technology develops. One can already see the effects in the political debates taking place regarding the development of the high definition television (HDTV) standards.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Low Bit Rate Image Coding
abstract: A motion compensated interframe prediction (MCIP) coder incorporating subband vector quantization is presented. The coder is based on two dimensional subband decomposition of the error image obtained after MCIP. The luminance and chrominance subbands, generated after the decomposition process, form image vectors which are then quantized using vector quantization. Low bit rates typically at 64 kbit/sec for videotelephony applications can be achieved by selecting only significant image vectors for transmission. A data compression algorithm that combines subband coding concepts and conventional VQ is used.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Approaches to image data compression for video coding
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Low Bit Rate Image Coding
abstract: Ideally a video codec should be cheap, small and available to a wide market. It should also make use of current telecommunications services that are widely available or will become available within a short time span. Such a service is the integrated services digital network (ISDN). In terms of bandwidth the provision of digital transmission over the subscribers' lines may be limited to 64 kbits/second. The advent of VLSI has led to low cost, high density devices for image processing becoming commercially available. However to achieve low complete system cost, application specific circuits are required. The design of such large silicon systems requires consideration of how well the algorithm maps onto the architecture.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Object-surface-based extraction and manipulation of 3-D medical-imaging data
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Low Bit Rate Image Coding
abstract: In acoustic, magnetic-resonance, or X-ray tomographic medical imaging, a number of slice cross-sections of elongated physiological structures are recorded, spaced relatively widely and nonuniformly along the object's longitudinal axis. Traditionally interpolation between the observed slices is used to assign an appropriate density value to each cubical voxel in 3D space. In generating pictures from this set of voxels, curve fitting is then used to reduce the measurement and spatial-quantization noise. Such interpolation and curve fitting implies well-defined and well-behaved interfaces between regions of distinct physiological tissue. By formulating these assumptions explicitly, the author can drastically reduce the data, to a compact representation of the interface surfaces. This avoids processing-generated spatial-quantization noise, and opens the way for highly efficient algorithms for data extraction, manipulation, and display.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Towards a theory of model-based image coding
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Low Bit Rate Image Coding
abstract: In model-based image coding, low bit rates are achieved by analysing a scene into moving objects and synthesising models which approximate them. The study reported is concerned with understanding the relationships between motion, shape and texture information in a model-based predictive coding system. The purpose of the study was to aid concomitant experimental work which sought to apportion bits in an optimal way between the three output bit streams; at present, due to model failure in only 4% of the image area, conditional texture updating information typically accounts for 80% of the total bit rate. The question therefore is whether model-based predictions can be improved without significant increases in the shape and motion information.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
